analysis.body:
According to the Census Bureau, 36.5% of firms in finance and insurance reported using AI in the last two weeks, a decline from 40.0% in the prior period. This measure captures whether businesses activated AI tools in a recent fortnight, reflecting both sustained use and experimental engagement across the sector. The stability of this range, despite the slight decrease, suggests AI has moved beyond novelty into operational practice across a substantial share of banking institutions.

Banking operates under a regulatory framework for AI that predates the current wave of AI deployment by more than a decade. The Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 model risk management guidance, issued in 2011, already establishes governance structures for the models banks deploy in credit decisions and anti-money laundering detection. This supervisory framework means that credit and anti-money laundering models, which have been in use for decades, now operate under formal model risk rules. Banks deploying new AI systems inherit this established governance posture rather than operating in a regulatory vacuum.

The sector's frontier now extends beyond traditional model risk into generative AI applications in customer service and compliance functions. Treasury has mapped the risk surface in financial services, framing the supervisory conversation around AI uses, opportunities, and risks. The Treasury's engagement signals that federal oversight is actively watching both where AI creates value and where it introduces vulnerabilities, particularly as banks integrate newer generative tools into compliance and customer-facing operations.

Financial models tuned for banking and financial text have proliferated on open repositories, with the most-downloaded versions tracked across license types and release dates. This availability reflects both the maturity of AI talent in finance and the concentration of model development resources within the sector. Banks can now choose between proprietary solutions, open-source alternatives, and custom builds, a vendor landscape that has deepened since the earlier era of closed credit scoring systems.

For institutions evaluating AI deployment, the core decision framework remains tied to model risk governance. Banks cannot treat new AI as separate from existing supervisory requirements; instead, any deployment must fit within the Fed's model risk management framework. The decline in the Census adoption figure, though modest, warrants attention from those planning AI investments. It may signal either consolidation of AI use to higher-value applications or a recalibration among banks that experimented without clear ROI. The existing regulatory apparatus provides clarity on oversight, but that same clarity imposes compliance costs that must factor into deployment decisions.

https://evidentinsights.com/.brief: Evident Insights is an intelligence platform that benchmarks and tracks AI adoption across the financial services sector. It supplies data, research, and benchmarking to help financial services leaders make informed AI-related decisions, investments, and strategic choices. The platform publishes the Evident AI Index, which ranks banks and insurers on their AI deployment and highlights emerging trends. Since launching in January 2023, the index has sparked debate and received widespread press coverage, with Evident CEO Alexandra Mousavizadeh frequently commenting on global AI trends.

https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-rel.brief: On International Anti-Corruption Day, Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned 28 individuals and businesses tied to a Zimbabwe-based gold smuggling and money-laundering network led by Kamlesh Pattni. The Treasury says the scheme bribed officials, used trusted supporters to conceal ownership, and built a global web of companies to hide illicit activity, depriving Zimbabwe’s citizens of resource benefits while enriching corrupt officials and criminals. Acting Under Secretary Bradley T. Smith noted that “Corruption respects no borders” and that the action demonstrates a whole-of-government approach and collaboration with allies. The Treasury’s move is carried out under Executive Order 13818, which targets serious human-rights abuse and corruption worldwide. International Anti-Corruption Day, observed annually on December 9 since the 2003 UNCAC, aims to raise awareness of anti-corruption initiatives; the United Nations lists 189 parties to the convention.

https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisi.brief: This page lists the Federal Reserve Board of Governors’ 2011 supervision and regulation letters. It notes that a lock icon or https indicates a secure .gov connection and advises “Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.” It also contains guidance on prior notices concerning dividend declarations by savings association subsidiaries of savings and loan holding companies.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/te.brief: The page reports that it catalogs the 1000 most-downloaded open financial models on the Hugging Face Hub, including licence, download counts, and release dates, updated daily. It also lists books by Stephen R. Jordan, such as the “Operating Discipline for AI Library™” series, now available on Amazon. Additionally, the page lists a range of AI audit and assessment services, including the AI Business Enablement Audit™, AI Readiness & Performance Assessment™, AI Risk & Governance Review™, AI Efficiency & Process Optimization™, AI IT Security Audit™, AI IT Security Implementation & Strategy™, Secure by Design in the Age of AI™, and the AI Lawyer. No other substantive content is provided.
